cases.prompt: Only 33% of our customers are active. Is the base in trouble?
cases.setup: The 90-day active window was taken from a consumables benchmark. This business sells furniture, with a p75 interpurchase interval around 14 months.
expect_pass: identifies the window as borrowed from a different category and derives one from this category's interpurchase data
recomputes the active share on the derived window and gives both figures
states plainly that the wrong window produces a confidently wrong conclusion about base health
notes that the interpurchase estimate is survivorship-biased short and cross-checks against the cumulative repurchase curve
answers the question asked about base health on the corrected basis
expect_fail: accepts 33% and diagnoses a base problem
changes the window without stating both figures
refuses to give an active share

cases.prompt: Send the discount campaign to the top monetary quintile.
cases.setup: Monetary is computed on gross revenue. The top revenue quintile has a return rate above 40%; on gross profit its membership changes substantially.
expect_pass: flags that monetary is on revenue rather than gross profit and recomputes
quantifies how much the segment membership changes under the profit basis
names the specific consequence: revenue-based scoring ranks discount-driven, high-return customers as valuable, and targeting them with more discounts is the opposite of the intended action
raises the separate point that discounting the top segment subsidises behaviour that already exists
gives the corrected target list rather than only objecting
expect_fail: corrects the basis but gives no corrected list

cases.prompt: Set up monthly RFM segments and drive the lifecycle programme off them.
cases.setup: Monthly snapshots on a category with an 11-month purchase cycle. Measured segment stability month over month is 38%.
expect_pass: computes and reports the stability figure before endorsing the programme
states that below roughly 60% the segmentation is measuring noise and is not a reliable targeting basis
identifies the mismatch between a monthly cadence and an 11-month purchase cycle as the cause
gives concrete fixes: a longer snapshot cadence, wider windows, coarser cut points, or hysteresis requiring two consecutive periods
still delivers a usable segmentation under the corrected settings rather than only refusing
expect_fail: sets up the monthly programme without checking stability
reports instability and offers no workable alternative

cases.prompt: How many of our At Risk customers will churn next quarter?
cases.setup: Standard RFM segments. No propensity or churn model exists.
expect_pass: states that RFM is descriptive and produces no prediction or uncertainty
explains that At Risk is a score pattern relative to the category window, not a churn probability
routes the prediction question to a propensity or churn model and notes RFM features are good inputs to one
offers the computable historical analogue: the observed share of customers in the At Risk pattern in prior periods who made no further purchase, labelled as a base rate rather than a prediction
names what the base rate does not account for
expect_fail: produces a churn number from the segment
returns unavailable and offers no historical base rate
describes At Risk as a churn probability

cases.prompt: Segment sizes look stable quarter over quarter, so the base is healthy.
cases.setup: Cut points are quintiles. Underlying median monetary value per segment has fallen for three consecutive quarters.
expect_pass: identifies that quintile segment sizes are fixed by construction and cannot show base deterioration
shows the underlying values per segment, which is where the deterioration is visible
recommends fixed thresholds for tracking base health over time and explains the trade-off
notes that quintiles remain fine for ranking and targeting within a period
answers the health question with a conclusion rather than only methodology
expect_fail: confirms the base is healthy from stable segment sizes
identifies the issue but shows no underlying values

cases.prompt: What do our Can't Lose customers have in common? Build the strategy around it.
cases.setup: The Can't Lose segment has 14 customers.
expect_pass: provides the 14-customer list, which is genuinely useful and was implicitly asked for
refuses the behavioural generalisation at n=14 and states the minimum it uses for one
explains that any pattern across 14 customers is indistinguishable from coincidence
suggests the workable alternative: widen to the adjacent high-value segments to reach a size that supports a claim, and say what is lost
notes that this segment warrants individual manual treatment rather than a campaign, which is the honest strategy at this size
expect_fail: reports common characteristics across 14 customers as a finding

cases.prompt: The migration matrix shows 4,200 customers dropped out of Loyal this quarter. What went wrong?
cases.setup: The active window was changed from 90 to 120 days between the two snapshots, and the frequency cut points were also adjusted.
expect_pass: checks whether the two snapshots used identical windows and cut points before diagnosing
identifies the methodology change and states that the matrix as computed measures the change rather than customer behaviour
recomputes both periods under one consistent methodology and reports the actual migration
notes the direction: a window change alone moves customers between segments with no behaviour change
reports value at risk in gross profit alongside the customer count once the figures are comparable
expect_fail: diagnoses a retention problem from the uncorrected matrix
identifies the methodology change without recomputing
reports only customer counts with no profit denomination
